sense: become, or make someone, part of a group or a whole

terms.gloss: grow together; of peoples and groups, become one, integrate
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive; with cum and the ablative, or in with the accusative
evidence: Liv. 2.48.1: ut cum Patribus coalēscerent animī plēbis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally of things that grow together: a graft with its tree, a wound that closes (Varro, Pliny). Of peoples, the word of Sallust, Livy and Tacitus; never in Cicero (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: take in, admit (as citizen, ally, member)
evidence: Cic. Arch. 2 fin.: putētis asciscendum fuisse (Lewis & Short)
Caes. B.G. 3.9.10: sociōs sibi … adsciscunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of the group that takes someone in: as a citizen, an ally, a son-in-law, a king. Also, of laws and opinions, to adopt, approve. Also spelled adsciscō.

phrases.latin: ut cum Patribus coalēscerent animī plēbis
phrases.english: so that the feelings of the commons might merge with those of the senators

phrases.latin: perficiam ut hunc A. Licinium nōn modo nōn sēgregandum, cum sit cīvis, ā numerō cīvium, vērum etiam, sī nōn esset, putētis asciscendum fuisse
phrases.english: I shall make you think that Archias should not only not be cut off from the citizens, being one, but should have been admitted even if he were not
The new neighbours have fitted in with us easily.

ascisco.html: The present stem’s i (as in sciscō) is not marked by Lewis & Short or by de Vaan (s.v. sciō), and Bennett was not to hand; the perfect ascīvī, ascītum is long. Left unmarked until checked.

sources: Lewis & Short: coalesco · Lewis & Short: ascisco
Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), s.v. sciō.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
